newsitem.title: THAILAND: Asia-Pacific may use more synthetic rubber - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Asia-Pacific may use more synthetic rubber - analyst.

text.p: Shortages of natural rubber in the longer term could lead to increased use of synthetic rubber in the Asia-Pacific region, an industry expert said on Tuesday.

Prachaya Jumpasut, chief economist of the International Rubber Study Group, said a shortage of natural rubber could be created by further industrialisation in major producing countries such as Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia.

"A shortage of natural rubber will lead to an increase in price and is likely to influence an increased development of synthetic rubber capacity in Asia-Pacific region," Prachaya told an international rubber conference here.
"For Asia-Pacific, natural rubber will continue to hold the larger share of consumption, but inevitably there will increasingly be higher and higher levels of synthetic rubber," he said.
Natural rubber currently accounts for 39 percent of global elastomer consumption.
The percentage of natural rubber consumption by the world elastomer industry fell from 55.9 percent in 1955 to 29.6 percent in 1979 before rising to 39 percent last year.
Total world rubber consumption has increased by an average of 3.8 percent a year over the past 40 years to reach 15.3 million tonnes in 1995, about 9.4 million tonnes of which was synthetic rubber.
In 2000, synthetic rubber consumption is likely to pass 11 million tonnes, according to industry estimates.
"This is an opportunity, not a cost, for this region to continue to maintain its leading role in the world elastomer industry," Prachaya added.

However, others said the role of natural rubber would continue to expand, reflecting the growth of rubber-based industries in producing countries, increased use in engineering applications and environmental concerns.
"When we talk about natural rubber consumption, in the back of our mind is always tyre industries," said Abdul Aziz, director of the Rubber Research Institute of Malaysia.
"But there will be exciting possibilities in the future because of increasing interest in using natural rubber for engineering applications," he told Reuters.
He noted that natural rubber accounted for 38-39 percent of all the elastomer consumption compared with an average of 32 percent several years ago.
"And we are confident that this will be increased in the future," he said, adding that natural rubber consumption could rise to 40 percent of total elastomer demand by the year 2000.
